Subject: The Evolution of Book Cover Design

Dear Valued Customer,

I hope this message finds you well.

Inspired by rising literacy rates and advancing technologies, the nineteenth century saw the book transform from a largely hand-made object to a mass-produced product. In this new context, a book's cover took on added importance: it was no longer merely a functional protection for the pages but instead a key platform through which to communicate and sell the book.

Prior to this, covers had — bar a smattering of highly bespoke one-off creations (e.g. embroidered covers for personal libraries) — mostly been plain leather bound affairs. From around the 1920s, the paper dust jacket — previously there to simply protect the publisher's binding — began to sport designs (and, of course, then paperbacks), but it was in the hundred years preceding, on these printed cloths, that book cover design first truly flourished.

Hi there,

I wanted to share a little something about Palitaw, a beloved native Filipino snack made with galapong (ground malagkit or sticky rice). If you're not in the Philippines like me, using glutinous rice flour is a great option for recreating it at home.

In some regions, you might also hear it called "dila-dila," a name derived from its oval shape that resembles a tongue (dila).

You've likely seen posts claiming that the Ministry of Power recommends setting your AC above 26°C for energy conservation and health benefits. While the intent is good, the facts tell a different story.

While the BEE correctly cited **energy conservation** as the rationale behind this move, they explicitly **did not mention any health issues** like hypothermia or arthritis as reasons for this regulation.

The claim that the Ministry recommends temperatures above 26°C for health reasons is **MISLEADING**. Stick to the official standards and set your AC to 24°C!

Subject: Reflections on Abraham Lincoln

Dear Valued Customer,

As Washington stands as the hero of the Revolution and the establishment of the government, so Lincoln stands as the hero of the mightier struggle by which our Union was saved.

Born in 1809, ten years after Washington, Lincoln's work done had been laid to rest at Mount Vernon. No great man ever came from beginnings which seemed to promise so little. Lincoln's family, for more than one generation, had been sinking, instead of rising, in the social scale. His father was one of those men who were found on the frontier in the early days of the western movement, always changing from one place to another, and dropping a little lower at each remove. Abraham Lincoln was born into a family who were not only poor, but shiftless, and his early days were days of ignorance, and poverty, and hard work.

Out of such inauspicious surroundings, he slowly and painfully lifted himself. He gave himself an education, he took part in an Indian war, he worked in the fields, he kept a country store, he read and studied, and, at last, he became a lawyer. Then he entered into the rough politics of the newly-settled State. He grew to be a leader in his county, and went to the legislature. The road was very rough, the struggle was very hard and very bitter, but the movement was always upward.

Sincerely,

Your Customer Service Team

That exasperating feeling of being accused of being exactly what you strive to avoid? William Hogarth knew it all too well. 👩‍🏫🎨

As an English artist of his time, Hogarth faced the derision of critics who labeled him a mere "caricature" artist. Far from accepting this slight, he was so moved by the ongoing misunderstanding that he created this 1743 print to explain the critical difference between characters and caricatures.

Hogarth saw these two forms as radically different:
🔹 **Caricature**: Defined by gross formal exaggerations and grotesque distortions.
🔹 **Character**: A comic representation that offers a subtle exploration of an individual's human nature.

For Hogarth, the latter was vastly superior. He firmly aligned his own style with the character, proving that true artistry lies in nuance, not just exaggeration.

What do you think? Is there a distinction you've encountered in your work that feels similar to Hogarth's? Let's discuss below. 👇

#ArtHistory #WilliamHogarth #CaricatureVsCharacter #GraphicDesign #ArtCriticism #CreativeProcess #1743

Dear Valued Customer,

As mapmakers began to gain a deeper understanding of the Earth's geography, some of the more playful among them, as well as those new to the art, turned their attention to charting more ambiguous lands. These artists created maps that depicted ideas as places and the machinations of the mind and heart as journeys.

Savor the rich, aromatic depths of this authentic lamb kofta recipe, masterfully blended with ginger, cumin, ground cloves, ground cinnamon, nutmeg, black pepper, cayenne, and salt. Start by combining these spices with 3 tablespoons of yogurt in a large bowl, mixing thoroughly before wetting your hands to shape the mixture into approximately 24 koftas—each 2-3 inches long and 1-inch thick.

In a large, heavy-bottomed (or cast iron) skillet, heat oil until hot. Sizzle in whole spices: a cinnamon stick, cardamom pods, whole cloves, and bay leaves. Once fragrant, add your meatballs in a single layer and fry on medium-high heat until lightly browned on all sides. For the signature sauce, beat the remaining yogurt with warm water, then pour this mixture over the meatballs. Bring to a boil, cover, and simmer for 30 minutes, turning the koftas every 8 minutes. As the dish cooks, the liquid will evaporate, leaving only a glossy layer of grease in the pan; if needed, crank up the heat to finish the process.

Remove the koftas with a slotted spoon, leaving the whole spices behind, and serve them hot alongside fluffy basmati rice.

Wet hands and shape mixture into approximately 24 koftas, 2-3 inches long and 1-inch thick. Heat oil in a large, heavy-bottomed (or cast iron) skillet. When hot, add whole spices: cinnamon stick, cardamom pods, whole cloves and bay leaves. Stir. Add meatballs in a single layer and fry on medium-high heat until lightly browned on all sides. Beat remaining yogurt and warm water. Pour yogurt-water mixture over the meatballs and bring to a boil. Cover, reduce heat and simmer for 30 minutes, turning the meatballs every 8 minutes. Too often, theorists mistakenly claim that character development belongs solely to drama, leaving the silent film to settle for mere "types." This is likely just a reflection of the crude state many current photoplays have not outgrown.

Internally, there is no reason why the visual language of the photoplay cannot depict complex, subtle characters. However, the core requirement remains clear: characters must remain consistent, driven by inner necessity and in harmony with the central idea of the plot.

But here is the critical point: insisting on unity gives us no right to focus only on the action that provides the content. We cannot make light of the form. Just as melody and rhythm are inseparable in music, every color combination has its limits in painting, and no stanza fits every idea in poetry, the photoplay must bring action and pictorial expression into perfect harmony.

This demand repeats in every single picture. We take it for granted that a painter balances forms perfectly, groups them to create internal symmetry, and ensures lines, curves, and colors blend into a unified whole. By the time we reach our years of discretion, we all possess a considerable number of moral maxims. We consider it wrong to steal, to lie, or to injure our neighbor. These maxims lie in our minds side by side, and we do not commonly think of criticizing them.

But now and then we face a situation in which one maxim seems to urge one course of action and another maxim a contrary one. Shall we tell the truth and the whole truth, when so doing will bring grave misfortune upon an innocent person?

And now and then we are brought to the realization that all men do not admit the validity of all our maxims. Judgments differ as to what is right and what is wrong. Who shall be the arbiter?

Not infrequently a rough decision is arrived at in the assumption that we have only to interrogate "conscience"—in the assumption, in other words, that we carry a watch which can be counted upon to give the correct time, even if the timepieces of our neighbors are not to be depended upon.

The German theory suggesting that Baldr could only be killed by his own enchanted sword—which Icelanders mistakenly interpreted as a mistletoe sprig—is far-fetched, romantic, and crumbles at the first touch. ai_draft: Directed by Walter R. Booth, this short stands as a wonderful example of early special effects, specifically the use of superimpositions where the "Lilliputians" are filmed on an oversized table-top set and then appear on screen alongside a normal-sized diner. The film features the same type of trick film as seen in J. Stuart Blackton's and Albert S. Smith's *Princess Nicotine*, which was made in 1909, eight years after *The Cheese Mites*. The producer of this example of early British cinema, Robert W. Paul (1869-1943), was an instrument maker who became involved in film when he was requested to build a copy of Thomas Edison's Kinetoscope, an early device for viewing films. As Edison's invention was not patented in Britain, Paul went on to build his own version of it, as well as making his own films since Edison's films were the only ones viewable on the machine. *The Cheese Mites* is the twenty-third film Paul was involved in, his earliest films having been made in 1895 and shown at The Empire of India Exhibition in London the same year. The following year, in 1896, Paul managed to build the "Theatrograph", a device which enabled a film to be shown on a screen and so viewable by a larger audience. See also Paul and Booth teaming up on the excellent short *Artistic Creation* (1901).

Known as the "Valley of the Shadow of Death," this photograph depicts a desolate scene littered with cannonballs, some filling a ditch and others scattered along a stretch of road. Subject: Emma Sutton explores Virginia Woolf and Music

Dear Valued Customer,

Last year, the works of Virginia Woolf entered the public domain in many countries around the world. To celebrate this milestone, Emma Sutton looks at Woolf's short story "A Simple Melody" and the influence which music had upon the writer who once wrote that music was "nearest to truth".

As Virginia Woolf's letters and diaries amply record, music was a central part of her social life as it was for many of her contemporaries, and she was at her best as a humorist writing about these occasions. She records with glee the various mishaps that befall musicians and audiences — a prima donna throwing down her music in a rage; a button popping off the plump Clive Bell's waistcoat during the slow movement of a piano sonata; an elderly man crashing loudly but astonishingly unhurt down the stairs at Covent Garden. The social conventions, artifice, and pretensions governing these performances intrigue her and allow her to sharpen her wit, but music wasn't only an occasion for slapstick humour or social satire. It played a central part in the political vision of Woolf's writing, shaping her understanding and representations of feminism and sexuality, pacifism and cosmopolitanism, social class, and anti-Semitism. And it informed, too, the formal experiments of her prose. Woolf learned many of her astonishing literary innovations from music — adopting from Wagner's operas, for example, the technique of shifting from one narrative perspective to another in order to represent the unspoken thoughts and feelings of her characters.

Best regards,

In a sense, *My Adventures as a Spy* is a last-ditch effort to resuscitate—or perhaps to preserve, like a butterfly pinned under glass—a mortally wounded world.

Discover the transformative power of boarding education, a tradition firmly rooted in our culture to correct the inequalities caused by individual homes. In our large public schools, life is meticulously designed to reshape character through two powerful forces: an ordered routine of discipline and, most importantly, the strong, shaping force of public opinion. This unique environment creates our schools' distinct character and profound effects.

Here, the student body collectively worships an idol they created: "Good Form." Public opinion establishes the moral code, setting a standard that is accessible yet demands excellence. Lying, sneaking, tattling, bullying, and "putting on side" are strictly forbidden as "bad form." While the definition of virtue may occasionally be nuanced—for instance, cheating to win a prize is unacceptable, but copying just enough to pass muster and avoid condemnation is forgiven—good form ultimately demands the highest social virtues.

We cultivate boys who are good fellows, easy to live with, and possess a high sense of public spirit. While these are the essential qualities of a well-rounded individual, our rigorous preparation ensures they are also ready to become the reformers and martyrs of the world.
human: I suppose it is for this reason that the custom of sending children to boarding-schools has so firm a hold among us. The boarding-school forms an environment selected to correct the inequalities which result from the special action upon the child of individual homes. The life of a boy in one of our large public schools is well calculated to act as a corrective in this way not only by reason of its ordered routine and discipline, but still more because it is affected, perhaps for the first time, by the strong force of public opinion. It is the strength of this public opinion which gives to our public schools their peculiar character and produces their peculiar effects. That which the schoolboy most despises is what he calls "Bad Form," and he bows down and worships an idol he himself has set up, the name of which is "Good Form." Public opinion forms the code of morals observed in the school. The standard set is commonly not so high as to be very difficult of attainment. It demands many good qualities. To lie, to sneak, to tell tales, to bully, to "put on side," are bad form. In some respects the definition of what is virtuous may be a little hazy. Thus it may be wrong to cheat to gain a prize, but to copy from one's neighbour only so much as will enable one to pass muster and escape condemnation is no great sin. In short, good form demands that a boy should have all the social virtues: that he should be a good fellow, easy to live with, and possessed of a high sense of public spirit--good qualities certainly, though perhaps not those which help to make the reformers or martyrs of this world.

Transfer the pan to a wire rack and allow the cupcakes to cool completely.

From West Africa to the heights of literary history: The remarkable journey of Phillis Wheatley.

Born around 1753 in present-day Gambia or Ghana, she endured the Middle Passage at just seven or eight years old before arriving in Boston, where she was sold as a domestic servant to John and Susanna Wheatley. Named after the slave ship that brought her, she was encouraged by her owners to learn, quickly becoming literate and writing poetry that soon appeared in local newspapers.

Despite facing significant prejudice based on her race, social status, gender, and age, Wheatley made history as the first published woman of African descent in 1767. She gained international recognition with her funeral elegy on the death of evangelist George Whitefield, addressed to his English patron, the Countess of Huntingdon, and published in both Boston and London in 1770.

By 1772, her growing transatlantic reputation led her to attempt to capitalize on it by producing a book of previously published and new works. Unable to find a publisher in Boston, partly due to racial prejudice, Wheatley and her owners successfully sought a London publisher and the Countess of Huntingdon's patronage in 1773 for her *Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral*.

The artist behind the image, and the man at the heart of the influential movement it came to represent, was Jan Toorop (1858–1928). Born on the island of Java in the Dutch East Indies, Toorop settled in the Netherlands at the age of eleven. After studying art at the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam, he spent his time between The Hague, Brussels, England (where his wife was from), and, after 1890, the Dutch seaside town of Katwijk aan Zee.

It was during this time that he developed his distinctive style: highly stylised figures embedded in complex curvilinear designs, with his dynamic line showing influence from his Javanese roots. While perhaps most famous for turning these techniques to his exquisite poster designs, Toorop also produced a substantial body of work far removed from the anodyne demands of the advertising industry—beautiful but haunting works dealing with darker subjects such as loss of faith and death.

Published in an oblong quarto format—typically reserved for musical scores and sewing patterns—Giegher's *Trattato* reflects the influence of tailoring. It notably anticipates later artistic movements, such as the work of Troublewit (paper animated by accordion folds) and ornamental orange peeling.

It would be easy to dismiss this craft as trifling, yet the diarist Samuel Pepys famously fantasized about paying a practitioner to teach his wife the art simply because he liked it so much. However, modern "virtuoso of the fold" Joan Sallas, who has recreated several of Giegher's *trionfi*, reminds us that these objects held *Sinnbilder*: symbolic meaning in German baroque.

Folding professionals were trained not only in technique and artistry but also in culture and the humanities, including recurrent themes like heraldry and mythology. In fact, Nuremberg once housed an entire school devoted to this art. Despite this, the craft was often practiced daily by servants—those "silent familiars of early modern households." As Deborah L. Crohn notes in her analysis of Giegher's manual, "their hands were allowed to speak with an eloquence that belied their status."
